conversation.content:
Hello there—thank you for coming in today. I’m Dr. Bennett, a clinician who specializes in helping new moms navigate the emotional ups and downs that can come after childbirth. I’m glad you’re here.

Over the next few minutes, we’ll use a quick screening tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s a set of 10 questions that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically during the past seven days. It isn’t a test, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever best describes your experience.

Everything you share is confidential, and our goal is to create a safe, supportive space where you can speak openly. After we finish the questions, we’ll talk together about what the results might mean and any next steps that could be helpful.

When you’re ready, we can start with the first question:

In the past week, when you thought about the future, how often did you feel able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

[Offering a small, tired smile]

I can still laugh—just not as easily as I used to. Maybe once or twice this week something made me chuckle, but it feels like I have to work harder to find the humor in things.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not very often... maybe once or twice, and even then it felt kind of forced. Things that used to crack me up before the baby now barely get a smile out of me.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[sighs softly]

Most of the time I haven’t. I used to get excited about little plans—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet evening. This week any time something comes up I catch myself thinking, “What’s the point? I’ll just be tired or the baby might fuss.” I did feel a spark of excitement when my sister mentioned dropping by, but it faded fast and I worried more about whether I’d have the energy to visit than about enjoying it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[Looking down at my hands]

Yes... a few times. When the baby wouldn't settle the other night, I kept thinking I must be doing something wrong—maybe I'm not feeding him right or holding him the way he needs. My partner said he's just fussy, but I couldn't shake the feeling that if I were better at this, he wouldn't cry so much.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[Pulling cardigan tighter]

A couple of nights this week I’d be rocking the baby at 3 a.m. and my heart just starts racing—no real reason. I keep checking that he’s breathing, worrying something will go wrong even though he’s fine. During the day it’s the same: I’ll suddenly think, “What if he’s not gaining enough weight?” even though the pediatrician said he’s perfect. I know it doesn’t make sense, but I can’t switch the worry off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[Twisting the edge of my sleeve]

A few times—mostly at night after I’ve finally got the baby down. All of a sudden my chest feels tight and my thoughts start racing, like something awful is about to happen, even though nothing’s wrong. It passes if I get up and walk around, but in the moment it feels like I can’t catch my breath for no real reason.
Things have been getting on top of me

[Exhales slowly]

Yes... most days. Between feedings, laundry, trying to sleep when the baby sleeps, and still feeling behind on everything, it piles up. Yesterday I almost cried just because I knocked over a bottle of pumped milk. I kept thinking, “I can’t even handle this one small thing,” even though I know logically it’s not a big deal.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[rubbing my eyes]

A few nights this week. I’ll finally get the baby settled, but then I lie there wide-awake, mind racing—going over everything I might have done wrong or need to do tomorrow. I’m exhausted, yet it takes me forever to drift off, and I wake up at the slightest sound even when my partner’s on shift.
I have felt sad or miserable

[Looking down, voice soft]

Yes… more days than not. It’s not constant tears or anything, but there’s this heavy, gray feeling that follows me around. I’ll be folding tiny onesies and suddenly feel like I’m on the verge of crying for no clear reason.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[Shakes head slowly]

Not really… I’ve felt like I could cry a few times, but only one night this week did I actually tear up. I was feeding the baby at 2 a.m. and just felt overwhelmed and alone, so a couple of tears slipped out, but it didn’t turn into full crying.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[Shakes head quickly]

No—never. I feel tired and low sometimes, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like myself again so I can take care of my baby.

You've shared how the joy and anticipation that used to come easily now feel distant, replaced by a heavy, gray mood that lingers most days. Simple tasks feel overwhelming, worries about your baby's safety race through your mind both day and night, and restful sleep remains elusive even when your little one is settled. Yet through it all you remain devoted to your baby and hopeful about feeling like yourself again.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 19, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports infrequent laughter that feels forced and diminished enjoyment compared to pre-baby, matching "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports almost total loss of anticipatory pleasure, consistent with anhedonia</sym>, <sym>Patient acknowledges self-blame "a few times" with persistent ruminations about parenting inadequacy, aligning with "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intrusive, uncontrollable worries occurring both day and night without valid cause, matching 'Yes, very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, unexplained panic episodes with tight chest and racing thoughts, happening "a few times" at night, matching "Yes, sometimes".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent daily overwhelm and inability to manage routine tasks, matching "sometimes haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes difficulty sleeping most nights this week due to racing mind and worry, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness "more days than not" and a persistent "heavy, gray feeling," aligning with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score ≥14 indicates probable major <med>depressive episode with peripartum onset</med>. Key markers include daily <sym>low mood</sym>, near-complete loss of interest (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), nightly <sym>anxiety</sym> and <sym>panic sensations</sym>, <sym>guilt</sym> about parenting, and <sym>middle insomnia</sym>. Symptoms present most of the past 7 days, causing functional impairment. No self-harm ideation (Q10=0). This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> within 1-2 weeks
2. Request formal assessment for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> and possible co-existing <med>anxiety disorder</med>
3. Discuss evidence-based treatment options: individual <med>CBT</med>, group therapy, or <med>SSRIs</med> compatible with breastfeeding
4. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to monitor symptom trajectory
5. Encourage 20-30 min daily outdoor walks and acceptance of household help to reduce overwhelm
6. Provide 24-h crisis line numbers and instruct to call if mood worsens or self-harm thoughts emerge
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 19: Postpartum Depression Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Self-report on the Edinburgh Postpartum Depression Scale (10-item) plus brief clarifications.

Symptoms endorsed  
– Persistent low mood, anhedonia, frequent tearfulness  
– Excessive self-blame/guilt re infant care  
– Unexplained anxiety, nocturnal panic sensations, intrusive worries about infant safety  
– Feeling overwhelmed, “can’t cope,” catastrophic reaction to minor stressors  
– Initial insomnia and middle insomnia despite severe fatigue  
– Passive death wish denied; no self-harm ideation, intent, or plan

Pattern  
Symptoms present most days for the past week, worse at night, not resolving with support or rest. Functional impact: difficulty completing household tasks, reduced social engagement, impaired sleep when infant is sleeping.

Screening significance  
Total score consistent with moderate depressive symptoms in postpartum period; anxiety symptoms prominent. Meets threshold for further evaluation for Major Depressive Episode with Peripartum Onset and comorbid anxiety. No current safety concerns identified.

Next step  
Recommend comprehensive psychiatric assessment (PHQ-9, GAD-7, clinical interview) and discussion of evidence-based treatment options.
